newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.

text.p: PM HEADING HOME SAYING TRIP EXTREMELY SUCCESSFUL
Prime Minister John Howard is on his way home from a two week overseas visit, which he's described as extremely successful.
Mr Howard has left New York saying he isn't worried by some negative media coverage of his trip.
The ABC's political correspondent travelling with the Prime Minister says there have been some hiccups.

She points to a stumble in the White House rose garden, Shirley MacLaine obviously struggling to stay awake at his foreign policy speech and, at his second last engagement, Mr Howard nearly dropping a model car presented to him by Mitsubishi.
But Mr Howard says the Australian people see the substance of the trip.
He has nominated the issue of Greenhouse gas emission targets as the highlight, saying with the US repudiating Europe's tough stand that alone justifies the time he has spent out of Australia.
The Prime Minister delivered an upbeat assessment of the Australian economy on the last day of his visit to the United States.
He told an investors' lunch in New York he's very enthusiastic about Australia's economic prospects.
Mr Howard told ABC Radio he's optimistic about what lies ahead, as the world is in an exciting and positive economic period.
He said there was a strong, vigorous and comprehensive story of economic achievement already and he thinks there are still better times ahead.
FEDERAL GOVERNMENT LAUNCHES "WINDOW ON THE LAW" SITE
The Federal Government has put information on Australia's legal system on the Internet.

The site, called Window on the Law, includes an overview of the Constitution, Australia's legal system and court structure, with access to Commonwealth legal material, laws, High Court judgements and publications.
Attorney-General Daryl Williams says it fulfils an election promise to provide Australians with universal access to the legal system.
Mr Williams says it's essential Australians have access to clear, understandable, user-friendly information on the legal system and the operation of laws that affect them.
He says the complex web of laws and regulations is a mystery to most Australians.
Mr Williams says people need to know and understand the law to benefit from its protection.
TEACHERS FIGHT BASIC SKILLS TESTS
Teachers are continuing to resist the New South Wales Government's planned basic skills tests, which would enable annual reports to be compiled on the performance of schools.
Six-hundred teachers at the Federation's annual general meeting voted unanimously yesterday to boycott the tests, because of concerns over privacy.
Federation President Denis Fitzgerald says teachers feel a duty to protect their students from sensational media reporting they believe the tests would lead to.
Mr Fitzgerald says there has been invasive reporting on HSC students in recent years.
He says earlier this year there was a particularly nasty form of reporting that was so disruptive teachers felt they had to ensure their children doing basic skills tests were protected.
Education Minister John Aquilina says his government remains committed to the basic skills tests, and will seek to negotiate further with teachers.
The minister says without the tests, it's impossible to bring down any school report that is in any way meaningful.
HANSON'S GOLD COAST LAUNCH TO BE SEEN IN ASIA
The Gold Coast launch of Pauline Hanson's One Nation Party last night will be shown on Asian Television programs.
Journalists flew out from Japan and Korea to cover the event, the first time Asian television stations have sent crews to one of Ms Hanson's meetings.
More than 1,000 people packed into the Gold Coast Arts Centre to hear the Independent Member for Oxley speak.
But they were forced to run the gauntlet of chanting protestors.
There was one arrest, but the demonstration was relatively peaceful.
Ms Hanson was ushered through a back entrance to avoid any confrontation.
A Korean Broadcasting System producer, Kang Taik Lee, says Pauline Hansen will feature in a 15 minute current affairs segment.
He says Koreans are becoming increasingly concerned about the race debate in Australia which he says could hurt Korea's national pride.
He also says the race debate will damage Australia's trading relations with Asia, if it continues, and Koreans are concerned that racism is rife in Australia.
HERPES DRUG TEST RESULTS DON'T MEAN A CURE SAY EXPERTS
An international group of experts on the herpes virus, says a recent experiment on an anti-viral drug should not be seen as a hope for a cure.
The study, conducted in England, showed that one drug stopped the reactivation of the sleeping, or latent virus, in herpes infected mice.

The Chairman of the expert group, Doctor Tony Simmons, from Adelaide's Institute of Medical and Vetinary Science, says there appears to be a worrying trend towards a belief that the results apply to humans.
Doctor Simmons says there was a possibility of affecting latency in mice, if they were treated very early with very large doses of antiviral compounds.

He says this is quite different to being able to treat people who have just become infected with herpes, because latency is established very early after infection, before the person even knows they've become infected.
